extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of theology, biblical interpretation, and political theology (educated Christian readers and scholars)
extracted.subtask_short: scriptural interpretation on afterlife and church
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a theological/political treatise arguing how Scripture should be read concerning the place and nature of eternal life, the meaning of Hell imagery, the definition and authority of the Church, and the relation of civil sovereignty to religious interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of eternal life / Kingdom of Heaven location
rubrics_metrics.description: The place wherein men are to live eternally after the Resurrection is to be determined from Scripture; the 'Kingdom of Heaven' refers to the kingdom of the King that dwelleth in Heaven, but the subjects need not ascend higher than God's footstool the Earth; ultimately the Kingdom of God (and salvation) is argued to be on Earth (Jerusalem) rather than a separate aetherial region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses John 3:13 and Acts 2:34 to show no textual necessity for bodily ascent to an Empyrean Heaven; distinguishes between Christ (who 'came down from Heaven') and ordinary men; appeals to Isaiah, Joel, and other prophets to place salvation emanating from Jerusalem on Earth; notes souls vs bodies distinction (souls may be with God prior to resurrection, but immortality of the whole man is by resurrection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immortality of the soul vs. immortality of the person
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture does not plainly teach that the soul's natural, inherent immortality makes any mere man immortal apart from the Resurrection; immortality of the man is granted by God's promise and the Resurrection, not as a natural property of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from Job 14 and 2 Peter 3 that human nature is mortal until the general Resurrection; distinguishes 'soul' and 'life' language in Scripture and asserts that patriarchs were immortal only by God's grace and promise (i.e., their election), not by natural necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret hell imagery metaphorically, not literally
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery used of Hell (under ground, Tartarus, lake of fire, utter darkness, Gehenna/Tophet) should be understood metaphorically rather than as precise literal geography or physical mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains each image's historical/origin basis (e.g., Tophet/Valley of Hinnon, Sodom and Gomorrah, Egyptian darkness) and shows they signify destruction, shame, exclusion, or purification rather than concrete spatial locations (no need to posit a bottomless pit in the globe of the Earth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of hellish torments (what the metaphors signify)
rubrics_metrics.description: Torments of Hell (weeping and gnashing of teeth, 'worm of conscience', fire, shame and contempt) denote grief, mental discontent arising from the sight of others' felicity and such bodily pains and calamities as occur under evil and cruel governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets biblical phrases (e.g., Matthew, Isaiah, Mark, Revelation passages) as depicting metaphorical states of grief, shame, comparative loss, and bodily calamity that may culminate in a 'second death' (everlasting destruction) rather than unending conscious life without possibility of death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satan, Devil, Abaddon are appellatives (offices), not proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: The names 'Satan', 'Devill', and 'Abbadon' are not intended as individual proper names but as titles/appellatives denoting an office or quality (Enemy, Accuser, Destroyer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues these words should have been translated rather than left untranslated in Latin and modern Bibles, because leaving them as names encourages belief in individual demons; when the Kingdom of God is on Earth, 'Satan' refers to earthly enemies of the Church.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Church (ecclesia) and its senses
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'Church' can mean: (a) God's house/temple (metaphorical for the congregation), (b) an assembly/congregation called by lawful authority (ecclesia legitima), (c) the whole multitude of Christians dispersed, (d) a particular part of Christians, or (e) the elect/Church Triumphant; properly it signifies an assembly/congregation in the classical civic sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains classical Greek/Roman provenance of 'ecclesia' and how usage varies in Scripture (1 Cor., Acts, Colossians, Ephesians, Matthew). Emphasizes the primary civic/assembly sense and its later extension to buildings and to the universal/elect senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful Church requires sovereign warrant; unlawful assemblies are not Churches
rubrics_metrics.description: A Church, when it is capable of acting as one person (to will, pronounce, command, make laws), must be assembled by lawful authority; assemblies without warrant from the civil sovereign are unlawful and their acts are not properly the act of the Church as one body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines a Church as 'A company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign; at whose command they ought to assemble, and without whose authority they ought not to assemble.' Asserts there is no universal earthly Church to which all Christians owe obedience because no single earthly power rules all commonwealths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil sovereign as chief pastor and interpreter of divine commands in the commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Christian commonwealth the civil sovereign occupies the role analogous to Abraham or a chief pastor: he alone (in the public, external order) determines what is to be accepted as the Word of God in that polity and may punish private revelations or doctrines contrary to the public religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draws analogy to Abraham's covenant (God spoke only to Abraham in that family) to argue that private visions or pretended revelations cannot override sovereign law; if pastors are not subordinate such that one chief pastor exists, contradictory doctrines and civil faction will follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redemption precedes Salvation; nature of the ransom
rubrics_metrics.description: Salvation of a sinner presupposes a prior redemption; the ransom required by God is not a monetary satisfaction equivalent to the offence but a sacrifice or price which God accepts—Christ's sacrifice is that ransom which God required for the salvation of repentant believers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between restitution for damage among men and pardon of sin (which cannot be bought in that sense); surveys Old Testament sacrifices and presents Christ's offering as the accepted price God demanded, not as a commensurate compensation making punishment unjust to impose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of general Salvation and 'World to Come' located on Earth (Jerusalem)
rubrics_metrics.description: General Salvation and the chief seat of God's Kingdom after Judgment will be on Earth, with Jerusalem as the focal seat from which salvation proceeds (Salvation 'is of the Jews'); the 'World to Come' corresponds to the promised new heavens and new earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports with Isaiah 33, Isaiah 66, Joel, Obadiah, and Jesus' remark to the Samaritan woman and Paul's 'to the Jew first'—interprets prophetic imagery as describing an earthly, lasting reign and restoration centered on Jerusalem and Mount Zion rather than an aetherial heavenly relocation of the faithful.
